outcome.answer:
You can determine compute requirements by measuring how model quality and efficiency change as you vary compute budgets, then fitting scaling laws or compute-allocation rules from those runs [2, 4, 6]. For recommendation systems, this means profiling low-level bottlenecks and estimating how much compute is wasted by inefficient modules, then using architectural changes that improve model FLOPs utilization and scaling efficiency [2, 5].

The supplied papers also show that inference compute can be reduced by sharing request-side work across many candidates, by caching summarized user history, or by redesigning attention and sequence modules to improve training and inference efficiency at scale [1, 9, 10]. If you mean “large scale suggesting systems” as recommender systems, these papers cover how to estimate and lower compute needs, but they do not give a single universal formula [1, 2, 5].
